pharm: Inactivated tetanus toxin that induces protective antitoxin antibodies against Clostridium tetani neurotoxin.
quick: 0.5 mL IM per dose; primary series plus boosters (combined as Td/Tdap where available)
Recommended; Td/Tdap given to protect mother and newborn
Compatible; may be given to breastfeeding women
Injection-site and systemic reactions; immediate allergic reaction post-dose
summary: Tetanus toxoid is an inactivated form of the tetanus neurotoxin used for active immunization to prevent tetanus (lockjaw). It stimulates production of protective antitoxin antibodies. It is given intramuscularly as a 0.5 mL dose, usually as part of combination vaccines (DTaP in children; Td or Tdap in adolescents and adults) rather than as a single antigen. A primary series is followed by boosters approximately every 10 years and after certain wounds. It provides active, long-lasting protection but does not treat established tetanus, which requires tetanus immune globulin.
indications: Booster immunization to maintain protection (routinely every 10 years)
Tetanus-prone wound management (with consideration of tetanus immune globulin in unimmunized/under-immunized patients)
Maternal immunization to prevent maternal and neonatal tetanus

dosage.d: Series of 0.5 mL doses per national schedule (e.g., DTaP at 2, 4, 6 months with later doses)
dosage.n: Tetanus toxoid given in combination products

dosage.d: 0.5 mL (as Td or Tdap) every 10 years
dosage.n: Tdap once for pertussis coverage, then Td/Tdap

dosage.d: 0.5 mL booster if >5 years (dirty wound) or >10 years (clean wound) since last dose
dosage.n: Add tetanus immune globulin if immunization status is uncertain/incomplete and wound is tetanus-prone

dosage.d: 0.5 mL (Tdap) typically in each pregnancy, per local guidance

admin: Administer 0.5 mL by intramuscular injection (deltoid in adults/older children; anterolateral thigh in infants)
Do not give intravenously or intradermally
Shake the vial to ensure a uniform suspension before withdrawing the dose
Have epinephrine and resuscitation equipment available for rare anaphylaxis
moa: Tetanus toxoid is tetanus toxin that has been chemically inactivated (detoxified, typically with formaldehyde) so it can no longer cause disease but retains immunogenicity. On injection it stimulates the immune system to produce anti-tetanus (antitoxin) antibodies. These antibodies neutralize the tetanospasmin neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani, preventing it from blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release at the neuromuscular junction and thereby preventing tetanus.

absolute: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose or to a vaccine component
Severe hypersensitivity to any constituent of the vaccine
relative: Moderate or severe acute illness (defer until recovered)
History of Arthus-type hypersensitivity after a prior tetanus dose (defer boosters to >=10-year intervals)
History of Guillain-Barre syndrome within 6 weeks of a prior tetanus-containing vaccine
monitor: Immediate hypersensitivity in the 15-30 minutes after injection
Neurologic symptoms in those with prior GBS

preg: Tetanus-containing vaccines (Td/Tdap) are recommended in pregnancy to protect the mother and provide passive protection to the newborn against neonatal tetanus; they are considered safe in pregnancy.
lact: Tetanus toxoid is compatible with breastfeeding and may be administered to nursing women; it does not pose a risk to the breastfed infant.
renal: No dose adjustment is required in renal impairment; immune response may be reduced in significant immunosuppression.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

moderate: Immunosuppressive therapy (corticosteroids, chemotherapy, biologics) may blunt the antibody response
Recent tetanus immune globulin can be co-administered at a separate site for wound management
minor: May be given with other routine vaccines at separate sites

serious: Severe local swelling of the limb

monitoring: Documentation of vaccination dates for booster timing
Neurologic symptoms in patients with prior GBS
counsel: Soreness, redness, or mild swelling at the injection site and a mild fever are common and settle in a day or two
Boosters are usually needed about every 10 years, and sooner for some wounds
This vaccine prevents tetanus; it is not a treatment if you already have tetanus
Tell the clinic if you have ever had a severe reaction to a tetanus shot
Keep a record of your vaccination dates
pk: Protective antibody develops over 2-4 weeks after the priming series
Antibody titers peak a few weeks after a dose
Antitoxin antibodies wane over years (immunologic, not pharmacokinetic)
Protection ~10 years after a complete series; boosters extend it
Store at 2-8 C; do not freeze; protect from light
pearls: Reference-sourced (CDC/WHO/SmPC) rather than from a single openFDA small-molecule label, as it is a biological vaccine usually given in combination (DTaP/Td/Tdap)
Toxoid provides active immunity; tetanus immune globulin provides immediate passive protection for tetanus-prone wounds in under-immunized patients
Do not give more often than every 10 years routinely to limit Arthus-type reactions
Does not treat clinical tetanus - that requires antitoxin/immune globulin plus supportive care
missed: If a scheduled booster or series dose is missed, give it at the next opportunity; the series does not need to be restarted - simply continue from where it left off.
overdose: Overdose is not clinically meaningful for a vaccine; inadvertent extra doses chiefly increase the risk of local (including Arthus-type) reactions. Manage symptomatically.
